## What the index measures {.unnumbered .unlisted}

The Anthropic Economic Index (AEI) publishes, release by release, how conversations with one provider's model spread across the tasks of the US O\*NET occupational database, and how each conversation divides the work: in an *automation* pattern the user hands the task over, and in an *augmentation* pattern the user works through it with the model. This paper calls the automation share *delegation*. It uses the releases from {{< var design.release.r1 >}} to {{< var design.release.r6 >}}, links tasks to occupations and occupations to the {{< var design.n_industries >}} Fama–French industries, and tests hypotheses fixed in a protocol registered as {{< var pap.tag >}} on {{< var pap.date >}}. {{< var meta.wording >}}

## Who delegates, and is it changing? (RQ1) {.unnumbered .unlisted}

The four hypotheses draw on research on trust in automation. The first, that delegation is lower in occupations requiring more education or paying higher wages (H1), is {{< var rq1.h1.decision_text >}}: within task families the automation share changes by {{< var rq1.h1.beta_e >}} percentage points per year of required education (interval {{< var rq1.h1.human_education_years_mean.ci_low >}} to {{< var rq1.h1.human_education_years_mean.ci_high >}}), and the wage coefficient points the opposite way from the prediction without being significant at its level. One pre-registered robustness row, R24 r5, brings the H1 test below its level; by design it changes no decision. The second, that delegation rises within the same task across releases (H2), is {{< var rq1.h2.decision_text >}}: the measured rise is one step between two releases followed by a fall, and the step coincides with a change in how conversations were classified, so classifier or platform drift cannot be told apart from behaviour; the balanced comparison also leaves out {{< var diag.h2.balancing_removed.n_tasks >}} tasks holding {{< var diag.h2.balancing_removed.usage_share_pct >}} per cent of usage. The third, that users check the model's work more where errors are costly (H3), is {{< var rq1.h3.decision_text >}}: the estimate is {{< var rq1.h3.gamma >}} percentage points of the checking share (interval {{< var rq1.h3.error_cost.ci_low >}} to {{< var rq1.h3.error_cost.ci_high >}}). The fourth, that countries differ in delegation beyond the mix of tasks their users bring (H4), is {{< var rq1.h4.decision_text >}}: holding task mix fixed, the automation share changes by {{< var rq1.h4.b1 >}} percentage points per unit of the log of the Anthropic Usage Index, a measure of usage relative to working-age population (interval {{< var rq1.h4.log_aui.ci_low >}} to {{< var rq1.h4.log_aui.ci_high >}}). Usage intensity and income are strongly correlated across countries, so their separate contributions are hard to tell apart, though the joint test is not.

## Could versus does (RQ2) {.unnumbered .unlisted}

RQ2 is descriptive and carries no test. Across the {{< var design.n_industries >}} industries, the rank correlation between delegation exposure and the human-rated theoretical exposure scores of Eloundou and co-authors is {{< var rq2.b.z_delegation.z_eloundou.rho >}}, with a bootstrap interval from {{< var rq2.b.z_delegation.z_eloundou.ci.lo >}} to {{< var rq2.b.z_delegation.z_eloundou.ci.hi >}} (@fig-rq2-could-vs-does): "could" and "does" order industries similarly. Three qualifications apply. Both measures use the same occupation-to-industry employment weights, so part of the agreement is shared occupational mix. Occupations the index does not publish are assigned zero usage by assumption, not measured as zero; dropping them instead lowers the correlation most, to {{< var rob.r03.spearman_z_eloundou_vs_z_delegation.estimate >}}. And the employment weights ({{< var vintage.oews.primary >}}) were published on {{< var design.s1.oews_release >}}, after the {{< var design.formation >}} formation date of the industry measures, so these are out of sample in AEI data only and not strictly real-time.

## Did markets price it? (RQ3) {.unnumbered .unlisted}

Rule D11 fixed in advance that market tests able to detect only implausibly large effects are reported as what the evidence can and cannot yet say. The smallest departure the main test could detect with {{< var power.power_pct >}} per cent power is {{< var d11.primary_mde >}} percentage points of annualised risk-adjusted return per standard deviation of exposure ({{< var rq3.h5b.mde >}} for H5b), above the pre-registered threshold of {{< var design.plausibility_pp >}} percentage points, so the rule applies. H5, that more delegation-exposed industries earned risk-adjusted returns departing from the historical pattern over the {{< var design.window.months >}} months from {{< var design.window.start >}} to {{< var design.window.end >}}, is {{< var rq3.h5.decision_text >}}: the estimated slope is {{< var rq3.h5.b_pp2 >}} percentage points per standard deviation, with an interval from {{< var rq3.h5.ci_005.lo_pp2 >}} to {{< var rq3.h5.ci_005.hi_pp2 >}}. H5b, that delegation exposure carries information beyond theoretical exposure, is {{< var rq3.h5b.decision_text >}}, with a slope of {{< var rq3.h5b.b_pp2 >}} (interval {{< var rq3.h5b.ci_005.lo_pp2 >}} to {{< var rq3.h5b.ci_005.hi_pp2 >}}). With employment weights public at formation (R32), the slopes are {{< var rob.r32.h5.estimate >}} and {{< var rob.r32.h5b.estimate >}} percentage points.

## What this does not show {.unnumbered .unlisted}

The index records conversations on one provider's platforms, classified by an unstated method that may drift across releases; it does not sample people at work and says nothing about the prospects of any occupation. The associations are descriptive: none says what would happen to usage or returns if delegation changed. The market non-rejections do not show that exposure is unrelated to returns, only that this short window had adequate power against departures from the historical pattern at least as large as the minimum detectable effect. Exploratory analyses, H6 among them, are labelled as such and are not findings.
